reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in the PTEN tumour suppressor gene, inherited autosomal dominantly, and forms part of the PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome spectrum
Characterised by multiple hamartomas across many tissues together with an increased risk of several cancers
Mucocutaneous features are highly characteristic and include trichilemmomas, oral papillomas (cobblestone mucosa), and acral/palmoplantar keratoses, often appearing by early adulthood
Confers elevated lifetime risks of breast, thyroid (typically follicular), and endometrial cancer, along with increased renal and colorectal cancer risk
Benign features include thyroid goitre and adenomas, gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps, uterine fibroids, and fibrocystic breast disease
Macrocephaly is common and, when combined with the cerebellar dysplastic gangliocytoma of Lhermitte-Duclos disease, is strongly suggestive
Overlapping PTEN-related conditions include Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome, and PTEN variants are associated with some cases of autism spectrum disorder with macrocephaly
Cancer surveillance targets the breast, thyroid, endometrium, kidney, and colon, with risk-reducing surgery discussed for breast and gynaecological risk
reference.pathophysiology: PTEN is a tumour suppressor phosphatase that antagonises the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling pathway, restraining cell growth, proliferation, and survival. Germline loss of PTEN function releases this brake, causing unchecked activation of growth-promoting signalling that produces widespread hamartomatous overgrowth and predisposes multiple epithelial tissues to malignant transformation. The same pathway dysregulation underlies the neurological features such as macrocephaly and Lhermitte-Duclos disease.
additionalDifferentials: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis (other hamartomatous syndromes)
Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (skin lesions and renal risk)
Neurofibromatosis and other tumour-predisposition syndromes with macrocephaly
additionalInvestigations: Germline PTEN sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Breast imaging (mammography with MRI) for at-risk women
Renal imaging and dermatological evaluation of characteristic skin lesions
redFlags: New breast, thyroid, or endometrial symptoms in a known PTEN variant carrier
Rapidly enlarging thyroid nodule suggesting carcinoma
Postmenopausal or abnormal uterine bleeding warranting endometrial evaluation
reference.prognosis: With structured multi-organ surveillance, cancers can be detected and treated early, and life expectancy is favourable when high-risk tumours are managed promptly. Prognosis is determined chiefly by the breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer risks, and lifelong follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Dismissing characteristic mucocutaneous lesions as incidental and missing the diagnosis
Overlooking macrocephaly as a diagnostic clue
Concentrating on one organ and neglecting the multi-organ cancer surveillance programme
Failing to offer cascade testing and counselling to relatives
